contextTopics.label: Russlands Krieg gegen die Ukraine
background: Russland überfiel die Ukraine am 24. Februar 2022 in vollem Umfang. Vorausgegangen war die Annexion der Krim im März 2014 und der von Russland unterstützte bewaffnete Konflikt im Donbas ab April 2014.

Die UN-Generalversammlung verurteilte den Angriff am 2. März 2022 mit 141 zu 5 Stimmen und forderte den sofortigen Rückzug. Die EU, die USA und weitere Staaten verhängten seither mehrere Sanktionspakete.
Der Internationale Strafgerichtshof erließ im März 2023 einen Haftbefehl gegen Wladimir Putin wegen der Verschleppung ukrainischer Kinder.
Österreich ist militärisch neutral, beteiligt sich aber an den EU-Sanktionen und leistet humanitäre Hilfe. Waffenlieferungen erfolgen nicht.

contextTopics.label: Krieg in Gaza und im Nahen Osten
background: Die Hamas verübte am 7. Oktober 2023 einen Großangriff auf Israel mit rund 1.200 Toten und etwa 250 Verschleppten. Israel begann daraufhin eine großangelegte Militäroperation im Gazastreifen.
Der Konflikt reicht weit zurück: Israel wurde 1948 gegründet, es folgten mehrere Kriege mit arabischen Nachbarstaaten. Der Gazastreifen wird seit 2007 von der Hamas kontrolliert.
Der Internationale Gerichtshof befasst sich seit Dezember 2023 mit einer Klage Südafrikas wegen mutmaßlichen Völkermords; ein Urteil in der Hauptsache steht aus.

Zahlenangaben zu Opfern stammen je nach Meldung von unterschiedlichen Stellen — der von der Hamas geführten Gesundheitsbehörde, israelischen Angaben oder UN-Organisationen. Sie sind selten unabhängig überprüfbar.

contextTopics.label: Handelskonflikte und Zölle
background: Die USA erhoben ab 2018 unter Präsident Trump Zölle auf Stahl, Aluminium und zahlreiche chinesische Waren. China antwortete mit Gegenzöllen. Teile davon blieben auch unter der Nachfolgeregierung bestehen.
Die EU ist als Zollunion für die Handelspolitik ihrer Mitgliedsstaaten zuständig — Österreich verhandelt also nicht selbst, sondern die Europäische Kommission.
Zölle wirken auf zwei Wegen: Sie verteuern eingeführte Waren für Verbraucher im Einfuhrland und treffen Exporteure im Ausland. Wer die Kosten trägt, ist wirtschaftswissenschaftlich umstritten.

contextTopics.label: Inflation und Zinspolitik der EZB
background: Die Europäische Zentralbank hat als vorrangiges Ziel Preisstabilität, definiert als 2 Prozent Inflation mittelfristig. Sie steuert darüber den Leitzins für den gesamten Euroraum.
Nach Jahren mit Null- und Negativzinsen begann die EZB im Juli 2022 mit Zinserhöhungen, um die stark gestiegene Inflation zu dämpfen — ausgelöst unter anderem durch Energiepreise und Lieferengpässe.

Österreich lag bei der Inflationsrate über Jahre über dem Euroraum-Durchschnitt. Die Gründe dafür sind umstritten; genannt werden unter anderem Energiepreise, Mietanpassungen und der Gastronomiesektor.

contextTopics.label: Klimapolitik und Klimaziele
background: Im Pariser Abkommen von 2015 verpflichteten sich fast alle Staaten, die Erderwärmung deutlich unter 2 Grad gegenüber dem vorindustriellen Niveau zu halten und 1,5 Grad anzustreben.
Die EU hat sich auf Klimaneutralität bis 2050 festgelegt und Zwischenziele für 2030 beschlossen. Österreich strebt Klimaneutralität bis 2040 an — früher als die EU-Vorgabe.

Der Weltklimarat IPCC fasst regelmäßig den Forschungsstand zusammen. Dass die Erwärmung überwiegend menschengemacht ist, gilt dort als gesichert; umstritten sind Tempo, regionale Folgen und Gegenmaßnahmen.

contextTopics.label: Regulierung künstlicher Intelligenz
background: Die Europäische Kommission legte 2021 den Entwurf für den AI Act vor, die weltweit erste umfassende Regulierung künstlicher Intelligenz. Er stuft Anwendungen nach Risiko ein und verbietet einige ganz.
Das Gesetz gilt für Anbieter, die ihre Systeme im EU-Markt anbieten — unabhängig davon, wo sie sitzen. Die Pflichten greifen gestaffelt über mehrere Jahre.
Kritik kommt von zwei Seiten: Teilen der Industrie, die Wettbewerbsnachteile befürchten, und Bürgerrechtsorganisationen, denen die Ausnahmen für Sicherheitsbehörden zu weit gehen.

contextTopics.label: Österreichische Innenpolitik
background: Österreich ist eine parlamentarische Demokratie. Der Nationalrat mit 183 Abgeordneten wird alle fünf Jahre gewählt; die Regierung braucht dessen Vertrauen.
Der Bundespräsident wird direkt gewählt, ernennt die Regierung und kann sie entlassen — eine Befugnis, die historisch selten genutzt wurde.
Untersuchungsausschüsse sind ein Minderheitsrecht: Ein Viertel der Abgeordneten kann einen einsetzen, ohne Zustimmung der Mehrheit.

contextTopics.label: Raiffeisen Bank International
background: Die Raiffeisen Bank International (RBI) ist eine der größten Banken Österreichs mit Schwerpunkt in Zentral- und Osteuropa. Sie ging 2010 aus der Fusion von RZB-Teilen und Raiffeisen International hervor.
Der Raiffeisen-Sektor ist genossenschaftlich aufgebaut: lokale Raiffeisenbanken, darüber Landesbanken, darüber die RBI. Diese Struktur erklärt, warum Entscheidungen oft mehrere Ebenen betreffen.
Das Russland-Geschäft der RBI steht seit dem Angriff auf die Ukraine unter besonderer Beobachtung von EZB und US-Behörden. Ein Rückzug wurde mehrfach angekündigt und verzögerte sich.

items.title: Scrum Day India 2026 Recap: Scrum Teams in the Age of Autonomous Agents
items.summary: Image On Saturday, 26 September 2026, Scrum practitioners gathered at To The New in Sector 144, Noida, for Scrum Day India 2026. The theme was Scrum Teams in the Age of Autonomous Agents . For the last two years, most conversations about AI in Scrum have been about assistance: a better first draft of a user story, a faster summary of a Sprint Review. This year's sessions started from a different place. Agents now pick up Product Backlog items, run checks, and produce Increments alongside the humans on the team. So the question was not whether Scrum still works. It was what Scrum Masters, Product Owners, and Developers have to do differently when part of the work is done by something that cannot be accountable. Seven practitioners answered that question across six sessions. Recordings and slides are going up session by session on the Scrum Day India 2026 session hub . Below is what each session covered, the threads that ran through all of them, and a few questions worth taking into your next Sprint Retrospective. The six sessions When AI Joins the Sprint: What Should Humans Stop Doing, Start Doing, and Never Delegate? Jaspreet Singh Chawla, Senior Business Analyst, To The New Jaspreet walked through what AI can now carry in each part of the work. In discovery it reads specification documents and Jira history to expose hidden dependencies and draft acceptance criteria. In refinement it flags ambiguous constraints and estimation risks. In development and testing it generates code iterations and builds test suites from past defect patterns. His answer to "so what do humans do?" is a five-part discipline for every AI-assisted workflow: See what the AI has already analyzed, Do only the work that needs judgment, Challenge outputs that look overconfident or incomplete, Stop manual work the AI handles reliably, and Own the final decision. The last one is non-delegable. Watch Jaspreet's session The Scrum Master's New Teammate: Autonomous AI Agents Shalini Khanna, Scrum Master, Coforge Shalini's opening line set the tone: AI is not taking Scrum Master jobs, it is removing the administrative comfort zone. Much of the tracking and documentation that filled a Scrum Master's week can now be handled by agents. What remains is the harder part of the accountability: coaching, risk mitigation, and improving flow. She showed two agents her teams use. An AI Release Coordinator connects to Azure DevOps and produces standardized, business-friendly release notes across teams. An AI Knowledge Partner pulls scattered knowledge from design documents, release notes, and user stories into one place. In her experience, it cut onboarding from weeks to days. Watch Shalini's session The AI-Native Software Team: From Personal AI to Autonomous Delivery Chetan Arora, Global Director – Enterprise Transformation & AI Strategy, Nagarro Chetan opened with a productivity paradox. He cited industry figures showing that most organizations use AI and most developers report personal productivity gains. Yet only a small minority see a financial payback within a year, or better team collaboration. His explanation: individual speed does not become business impact until the delivery system itself changes. He described three levels, AI for Me, AI for Engineering, and AI for Delivery. When code generation gets faster, the bottleneck moves upstream to discovery and planning, and downstream to testing and release. His model sorts work on a scale from human judgment to AI autonomy. Humans keep vision, strategy, trade-offs, and accountability. AI augments analysis. Agents take bounded tasks with explicit guardrails. Rule-based routine work is automated. Watch Chetan's session KPI Blueprint for Agentic AI Workflows Deepti Jain, Agentic Workflow Specialist Deepti made the case that chatbot metrics fail for agents. A chatbot is judged one response at a time. An agent plans, calls tools, and executes multi-step work, where one error can break a workflow or change data. She proposed KPIs in three tiers: operational (autonomous completion rate, human escalation rate, cycle time), technical and financial (tool accuracy, LLM cost per completed task), and business impact (net human hours saved and a "Trust Curve" for how much oversight an agent still needs). Her cost section was the most practical of the day. Agentic loops often run 5 to 15 internal turns, and each turn resends the growing history, so a single query can consume tens of thousands of tokens. Her fix is model cascading: a premium model plans and reviews, smaller models handle sub-tasks. In her example, cost per task fell by more than half at the same accuracy. Watch Deepti's session When Half of Your Team Is AI Agents Sanjay Saini, Professional Scrum Trainer and Founder, AgileWoW My own session looked at the Scrum framework itself. What happens to the Scrum events and artifacts when a Scrum Team provisions five AI coding agents next to its Developers? Sprint Planning needs an explicit decision about…

items.title: 5 Things the Scrum Master Shouldn’t Be Doing
items.summary: Image I love being a Scrum Master. What I love about it is helping a team accomplish something and honestly just making Developers' work lives as hassle-free as possible. I love working with smart people and seeing them accomplish amazing things. As a Scrum Master, most of us want to help. But sometimes we think we are helping when we’re actually hurting the team. As a case in point, when I was a new Scrum Master, I was looking for how to add value to the team. So, I observed that submitting security and access requests was an annoying administrative job for the Developers. I suggested that I could help take those over for Developers. What began as a way to help quickly became a bottleneck. Pretty soon one of the Developers asked me, in an annoyed tone, if they had to submit these through me because it would be faster just to do it themselves. It was a lesson I haven’t forgotten. Sometimes helpfulness can be annoying. Sometimes knowing what NOT to do can be as helpful as knowing what TO do. Here are five things that the Scrum Master shouldn’t be doing. 1) Gatekeeper No, I’m not talking about security access again. I once worked at an organization where instead of being the Scrum Master I was a stakeholder. I needed to request work from the Scrum team, and I knew it was a quick five-minute job, so I emailed my request to the Product Owner. Instead of adding the request to the Product Backlog (or telling me “no”), I got a snippy email from the Scrum Master a week later telling me that all requests for the Scrum team had to go through her. I decided to play by her rules and sent her a reply with my request, explaining that it was urgently needed. Ten back-and-forth emails and a couple of unanswered calls later, I finally actually gave up. Some months later I received an email from a Developer asking for details about my request. I was surprised because I didn't know my work request had even been added to the Product Backlog, so by that time the business had developed a work-around. What I remember about this request was not so much the request itself but the frustration and lack of visibility around working with that Scrum team. 2) Organizing the Scrum Team into teams I observed a Scrum Master once who was working to roll out Scrum to a new area of the business. One of the managers (who didn’t work directly with that team) met with other executives (who also didn’t work directly with those team members) and they put a lot of thought into how the teams should be structured and who should be on each team. It was well intended and well thought-out, but totally unnecessary. A better approach would have been to let the team self-organize. On the many occasions where I have let teams self-organize, they mostly don’t come up with anything different or better or worse than what executives would have come up with. (Well, to be honest, usually it’s a bit better than what the executives would have come up with.) But the important thing is that they make it work because it was their own idea. And that makes all the difference. I did this once with a team of sixty people remotely. They came up with their team structure, and they were empowered to decide who would be on each team. It improved morale. It made them feel in control of their own work. And it made them more collaborative than they otherwise would have been. Six months later, when priorities changed, they decided one day at a Retrospective that they needed to re-organize to meet the new business needs. And so they did. No management intervention needed. 3) Making decisions for the Scrum Team If your team is facing a larger decision, it isn’t up to the Scrum Master to navigate this for them. What the Scrum Master can do is bring together the team members for a discussion and let them decide how to accomplish it. For example, if the team is doing some greenfield development and they need to make a major architectural decision, I have often had Developers ask me to schedule a meeting to bring the right people together to discuss it. I facilitate the meeting in such a way as to make it productive. That’s my part as the Scrum Master. But I don’t make the decision for them. If they need to request approvals from higher-ups due to it being a significant decision, I ask how they want to go about that. Usually, it’s a follow-up meeting with leadership. 4) Owning the Sprint Review Now this one is a bit nuanced. As the Scrum Master, it is my job to ensure that the Scrum events are positive, productive, and kept within the timebox. But the Sprint Review is the Product Owner’s most valuable event. They really need to take a starring role here, so it's important that I as the Scrum Master don't take over this event. I’m not saying that the Product Owner has to lead the whole thing personally. In fact, it is really better if, during the part where we are inspecting the Increment, Developers can lead the discussion and get feedback on their own work, where appropriate. But the…

items.title: Outcome-Based Leadership in Project Management: Measuring What Really Matters
items.summary: Image The Context I once led a software development program with more than 100 developers and several project managers. The projects were strategically important for the company, and expectations from upper leadership were high. Officially, the organization was working with Scrum. In practice, however, the organization was following a waterfall approach. Upper leadership was not satisfied with the program's performance. Project managers were also under increasing pressure to improve their individual performance. My mission was clear: get the program back on track and help the project managers reach a higher level of performance. But one question quickly became apparent: What exactly does good project management performance mean? The Problem: Measuring the Wrong Thing When asked how project manager performance was measured, top management struggled to provide a clear response. The answer usually came back to familiar project success metrics: On time. In budget. In scope. These metrics can be useful in managing project success (while usually falling short of adequately measuring project success). But they are not sufficient to evaluate project management performance. A project can miss a deadline because of changing customer requirements, technical challenges, organizational dependencies, or decisions made far outside the project manager's area of influence. Conversely, a project can remain on schedule and within budget while communication is poor, risks are hidden, and stakeholders are constantly surprised by what happens next. Project success and project management performance are related, but they are not the same thing. That raised a more fundamental question: If project managers should be led based on the outcomes produced, what is the actual outcome of project management? It obviously cannot be project success alone. Finding the Real Outcome I started looking for the answer by talking to the people involved. Stakeholders and project managers were asked a simple question: “How do you know that project managers are performing well and delivering great outcomes?” The “Five Whys” technique helped dig deeper: Whenever an answer described an activity, result, or indicator, the question was asked again in a slightly different form. The answers gradually moved away from project management activities and toward the actual experience of stakeholders. The surprising result was not to “keep the projects on schedule.” The more meaningful outcome was to “keep the number of unpleasant surprises down.” That was a breakthrough. Measuring Unpleasant Surprises In this particular context, reducing unpleasant surprises turned out to be a surprisingly powerful measure of project management effectiveness. Stakeholders became frustrated and pressure increased whenever unexpected information arrived unanticipated. The problem was not necessarily a changed timeline as such. For example, a stakeholder asking for an additional feature might make a milestone move. For them, this scenario did not automatically indicate poor project management. However, a last-minute confession that the team had already known for six weeks that the milestone would have to move posed a huge issue for these stakeholders. The difference is enormous. A changed timeline revealed at the last possible moment creates a surprise, destroys trust, and leaves little room for meaningful action. With this insight being clear, the program started measuring the number of unpleasant surprises per week. The measure was deliberately simple. Whenever I as the program manager was surprised by information that could reasonably have been known or communicated earlier, the situation was captured and discussed. The goal was to identify possible transparency and communication improvements. This changed the focus of project management. Instead of primarily asking: “Are we still on schedule?” the conversation increasingly leaned towards: “Does everyone who needs to know have the information needed to make good decisions?” From Measurement to Better Leadership The new focus created a much more useful basis for leading the project managers. Fewer unpleasant surprises meant better transparency, leading to earlier inspection and more opportunities for adaptation. Earlier adaptation increased the chances of achieving successful project outcomes. Schedule, budget, scope, quality, and other project metrics remained important. The difference was that these metrics were no longer treated as a direct proxy for project manager performance. Instead, the project management outcome became more closely connected to creating transparency and predictability for the people who depend on the project . The Takeaway Identifying the right outcome is not always easy. Especially in complex environments, it can be tempting to use easily measurable project metrics as a substitute for understanding the actual contribution of project management. items.title: Not All Complexity Can Be Processed Away. Fred Brooks Proved This in 1986.
items.summary: Image Every struggling product organization I sit with arrives at the same prescription: add more process, a pre-sprint refinement session, a mid-sprint review, more documents, more sign-offs, better status visibility. I have watched this pattern since 2010, and it almost never works. Most of what those organizations are dealing with cannot be fixed that way. The distinction was drawn by Fred Brooks in 1986, in a paper called "No Silver Bullet," delivered at the IFIP Tenth World Computing Conference. Brooks borrowed the framing from Aristotle, who separated essence from accident. Accidental difficulties "attend production but are not inherent" in the work. Essential difficulties are "inherent in the nature of the software." The first kind can be removed by better tooling, better languages, better process. The second is just what the work is. What Accidental Complexity Looks Like Brooks spent much of the paper locating past productivity gains in the accidental category. High-level languages removed the difficulty of mapping abstract intent onto machine instructions, delivering roughly a factor-of-five gain. Each gain was real but limited to removing what Brooks called "artificial barriers." Product work has its own supply of accidental complexity: backlogs with 300 items nobody navigates, release processes needing a week of setup per deployment. Another form is the steering committee sign-off that holds up development on work the team already understands. Better tooling, a trimmed backlog, tighter meetings reduce friction without changing the core work. Most product organizations know how to find gains in this category. The trouble is that fixing accidental complexity is real progress. That makes it easy to reach for when the actual problem is essential complexity. The Four Essential Difficulties Essential complexity cannot be removed without changing the problem. Brooks named four properties of software that resist simplification, and all four appear in product development. Complexity is the first essential difficulty Brooks named. Software entities are "more complex for their size than perhaps any other human construct, because no two parts are alike," and every scaling adds new kinds of elements, not just more of the same. Every product is a different answer to a different problem in a different context. Conformity is the second essential difficulty Brooks identified. Software must conform to interfaces it did not design; Brooks called this complexity "forced without rhyme or reason by the many human institutions and systems to which its interfaces must conform." For a product team this is the legacy infrastructure that limits what is deliverable. It is the legal requirement that arrives mid-Sprint, or the enterprise contract that specifies the API shape before the product is built. None of it simplifies out from the product side. The third essential difficulty, changeability, follows from success. Brooks described software as "pure thought-stuff, infinitely malleable," which means every successful product faces constant pressure to change as users invent new uses and markets shift. The pressure does not ease when planning becomes more detailed. Brooks named the fourth essential difficulty invisibility. A building has a floor plan; a circuit has a schematic. Software "has no ready geometric representation," and neither does the product problem it is meant to solve. Assumptions stay hidden until a Sprint Review proves them wrong, and dependencies only surface when they break. No process makes hidden things visible; it can only help them surface faster. A Counterargument The easy objection is that Brooks was writing about 1986-era software projects, not modern product management. That objection is fair on the specifics. False on the structure. All four essential properties appear in product work, because product work is also building abstract constructs in changing contexts. The properties follow from that, not from the decade. Why This Explains the Protocol and the Agenda I wrote recently about Scrum's two layers: a prescriptive, auditable protocol and an agenda that sets outcomes without specifying steps [3]. Brooks' framework shows what each layer is doing. The protocol does two things, and most teams only notice one. It reduces accidental complexity by governing choices that do not need judgment: fixing the Sprint length, respecting the timeboxes, defining the artifacts. And it builds structure that forces teams to confront essential complexity. The Sprint boundary limits how far changeability can compound before you inspect. The Sprint Review surfaces invisibility: hidden assumptions have to survive real use before the next Sprint. The protocol does not resolve the four essential difficulties. It makes them visible on a short enough schedule to respond. The agenda is discovering what users need and delivering it. That is where essential complexity has to be faced. You cannot specify value in advance;…

items.title: Does Your Organisation Need an AI Product Owner?
items.summary: Appointing one person accountable for AI is a sound first step. In an organisation moving to a product operating model, or already running one, the same role puts a dependency and a handoff between product teams and the decisions the model gives them. Most organisations adopted AI before anyone was accountable. Pilots started in several teams at once, and whichever area needed them first bought the licences. When an AI output went wrong, nobody could say who was accountable. In a 2026 BCG survey, half of respondents said their companies lacked clear governance for teams of people and AI, and almost as many named AI accountability among their three top concerns (Martin et al., 2026). Appointing an AI Product Owner gives the organisation one person who can make AI decisions, while ISO/IEC 42001 sets the same expectation: top management must ensure that responsibilities and authorities for the roles in an AI management system are assigned and communicated (International Organisation for Standardisation [ISO], 2023). As a first step, the role works. Executives know whom to ask about AI, and one person collects lessons from separate pilots instead of losing them when each pilot ends. The difficulty starts when the first step becomes the permanent design. Once an organisation commits to a product operating model, in which persistent product teams are accountable for outcomes (Cagan et al., 2024), an AI Product Owner holds the decisions the model assigns to each product's Product Owner, and every team that adopts AI adds to that one person's queue. Capable organisations create the role for a structural reason. When a new technology is adopted, the familiar response is to set up a function for it and appoint someone to run that function, because a project-funded organisation has no persistent product that could own the technology. The AI Product Owner is that response with a Scrum title. Manufacturers took the same path with quality: inspection departments checked work after it was done, until Deming (1986) argued that quality had to be built into the production process rather than inspected afterwards. AI is rarely a product The Scrum Guide makes the Product Owner accountable for maximising the value of the product that results from the Scrum Team's work. The Product Owner is also accountable for effective Product Backlog management: developing the Product Goal, creating and ordering Product Backlog items, and keeping the Product Backlog transparent (Schwaber & Sutherland, 2020). The Scrum Guide describes a product as a vehicle to deliver value, with a clear boundary, known stakeholders and well-defined users or customers. Its Product Owner is "one person, not a committee", and succeeds only when the whole organisation respects their decisions. AI fails that definition in most organisations. It sits inside many products and has no boundary of its own; its stakeholders are everyone, and its users are teams already building other products. An AI Product Owner therefore holds no product in the Scrum Guide's sense, only an interest in how every other product is built. That interest conflicts with the Product Owners who already exist. Consider a team building a claims service, whose Product Owner is accountable for the value that service produces. If an AI Product Owner also decides how the team uses AI, what it prioritises or what it may release, the team answers to two people. When their decisions disagree, the organisation cannot respect both, so the Scrum Guide's condition for an effective Product Owner fails for at least one of them. What the role costs product teams The first cost is that accountability turns back into coordination. Evolve argues that better coordination between organisational units changes how those units work together but leaves unchanged what each one answers for (Hodgson, 2026). An AI Product Owner who negotiates AI priorities with every Product Owner is a coordination mechanism carrying an accountability title. When several managers hold partial authority over what an AI-augmented team releases, contested outputs produce meetings rather than decisions, and releases wait until everyone agrees (Hodgson, 2026). The second cost is an extra handoff, added where AI makes handoffs most expensive. AI shortens the time spent on active work but leaves the waiting time at each organisational boundary unchanged, so the share of total cycle time spent waiting rises (Hodgson, 2026). Each team that adopts AI adds requests to the AI Product Owner's queue, and the wait at that boundary lengthens with every team that joins. Reinertsen (2009) identified unmeasured queues of this kind as the main cause of long cycle times in product development, and a checkpoint with no accountability adds queue length without adding anything to the Increment (Hodgson & West, 2026). Es ist eine Haltung, die als „Rückstandsgeheimnis“ angesehen wird. Kein geschäftlicher Markt – unter Effizienzdruck, verzweifelter Anstrengung und finanzieller Belastung –, es ist veraltet. Um Produkte nachhaltig zu konstruieren und Geschäfte mit der Autorin abzuschließen, oder ein professioneller Produktprofi, der sich mit der Disziplin eines erfolgreichen Dojos für Product Ownership beschäftigt. Nach dem ersten Schritt – von Faixa Verde zu Faixa Marrom und schließlich zu Faixa Preta –, einer radikalen Mentalität: Ich war besessen davon, mit der Menge an Einsendungen zu beginnen und mich in das Reich der Entdeckungsreise zu begeben, aus wirtschaftlicher Sicht und mit der Strategie des Marktes. Auf dem neuen Wettbewerbsvordergrund sind jedes Jahr junge Erwachsene von einem künstlichen Intellektuellenpiloten angetrieben worden. Bild 1. Ich habe die Stakeholder nicht mit Fragen zu den Grundproblemen betraut und bin mir sicher, dass wir uns so schnell wie möglich darum kümmern müssen, ihnen weiterhin verzweifelte Fragen zu stellen. Kein Problem und keine Probleme: Ich habe mich immer direkt für eine Lösung entschieden, habe den Kunden die Möglichkeit gegeben, Gelegenheiten zu nutzen und zusammengestellte Experimente zu erstellen, um kritische Prämissen zu validieren, bevor ich mit der Arbeit arbeite. Reduzierung des Nutzungs- und Valor-Risikos: Wir haben uns die Zeit für das Design und die Prüfung genommen, um zu garantieren, dass das Produkt gebrauchsfähig, funktionstüchtig und originalgetreu ist. O Apoio da IA ​​no Nível Verde (O Robô de Discovery): O Faixa Verde nutzt autonome Agenten, um hunderte von Kunden, Support-Tickets und Rückmeldungen von Benutzern innerhalb von Minuten zu bearbeiten. Ich bin ein Assistent, der in der Lage ist, Padrões zusammenzufassen, Hip-Hop-Aufgaben zu erstellen (Problemstellungen) und dabei zu helfen, schnell spezifische Funktionen zu erstellen, den PO freizugeben, um sich auf die Durchführung und die menschliche Interaktion mit den Kunden zu konzentrieren. Bild 2. Faixa Marrom: Das wirtschafts- und wirtschaftsstarke Unternehmen Validar Hipóteses and Entregar Solutionscom boa Usabilidade não basta se o produto queima caixa sem gerar no retorno to reto investido. Faixa Marrom übernimmt die Verantwortung für die Finanzierung durch die Initiative und verbindet den Rückstand direkt mit der Ergebnisdemonstration ( P&L ). Gewinn- und Verlustrechnung, Margen und Bewertungsstrategie: O PO dominiert die Zusammensetzung der Direktverwalter (COGS), brutale Marge und operative Lukrativität. Wir verstehen, wie jede Funktionalität oder jedes Modell der Präzision (Preisgestaltung) den Fluss der Ware und die Marge des Beitrags zum Verhandlungsergebnis beeinflusst. Unrealisierter Wert (UV): Die Gelegenheit und die Tatsache, dass der Markt nicht erfasst wurde. Time-to-Market (T2M): Die Geschwindigkeit, mit der der Zyklus zwischen einer Produktlinie, der Produktion und dem Verkauf abgeschlossen wird. Fähigkeit zur Innovation (A2I): Die Fähigkeit zur Innovation scheint durch die Belastung technischer oder bürokratischer Prozesse gesichert zu sein. Die Ergebnisse der IA auf Nível Marrom (Dashboards Predictions e Analytics): Die Faixa Marrom arbeitet mit Modellen der IA-Vorhersage, die die Auswirkungen von Preisschwankungen, Projekten oder Gewinn- und Verlustrechnungen in der realen Zeit simulieren und Anomalien auf den EBM-Metriken erkennen, bevor sie während des Trimesters verunreinigt wurden. 3. Faixa Preta: Eine Vision des Unternehmers, Três Horizontes und ein Brückenkopf auf der Faixa Preta, der Product Owner, der von Ralph Jocham und Don McGreal als Geschäftsführer beschrieben wurde: o PO als erfolgreicher Unternehmer und Risikomanager. Bei der Eroberung neuer Märkte wurde das Gleichgewicht zur Unterstützung des Handels präsentiert. items.origTitle: O Dojo de Product Ownership: Gestão Avançada de Produtos na Era da Inteligência Artificial
items.origSummary: A maioria das organizações ainda encara a gestão de produtos como uma linha de montagem: escrever histórias de usuário, alimentar o backlog, acompanhar a velocidade das sprints e torcer para que a funcionalidade entregue gere algum resultado. Essa postura é o teto de vidro do "PO secretário de backlog". No mercado corporativo atual — pressionado por eficiência, corte de desperdício e impacto financeiro —, essa abordagem tornou-se obsoleta. Para construir produtos sustentáveis e liderar negócios com autoridade, o profissional de produto precisa trilhar a disciplina de um verdadeiro Dojo de Product Ownership . Conforme a graduação avança — da Faixa Verde à Faixa Marrom e, finalmente, à Faixa Preta —, a mentalidade muda radicalmente: sai a obsessão pelo volume de entregas e entra o domínio do discovery ágil, da saúde econômica e da estratégia de mercado. E, na nova fronteira competitiva, cada um desses graus de maturidade é impulsionado por um copiloto de Inteligência Artificial. Image 1. Faixa Verde: O Domínio do Discovery e da Validação Rápida O Faixa Verde é o profissional que rompeu definitivamente com a fábrica de entregas cegas ( build trap ). Ele não aceita pedidos de stakeholders sem questionar o problema de fundo e sabe que construir a coisa errada rapidamente continua sendo um desperdício. Foco no Problema e em Hipóteses: Em vez de pular direto para a solução, mapeia dores reais dos clientes, desenha árvores de oportunidades e estrutura experimentos enxutos para validar premissas críticas antes de acionar a engenharia. Redução de Risco de Usabilidade e Valor: Trabalha integrado ao time de design e pesquisa para garantir que o produto seja usável, viável e genuinamente desejado. O Apoio da IA no Nível Verde (O Robô de Discovery): O Faixa Verde utiliza agentes autônomos para processar centenas de entrevistas, tickets de suporte e feedbacks de usuários em minutos. A IA atua como um assistente incansável que sintetiza padrões, gera rascunhos de hipóteses ( problem statements ) e auxilia na criação rápida de especificações funcionais, liberando o PO para focar na escuta ativa e na interação humana com os clientes. Image 2. Faixa Marrom: O Domínio do Valor Econômico e da Eficiência Validar hipóteses e entregar soluções com boa usabilidade não basta se o produto queima caixa sem gerar retorno sobre o capital investido. O Faixa Marrom assume a responsabilidade pela saúde financeira da iniciativa, conectando o backlog diretamente à demonstração de resultados ( P&L ). P&L, Margens e Estratégia de Precificação: O PO domina a composição de custos diretos ( COGS ), margem bruta e lucratividade operacional. Ele compreende como cada funcionalidade ou modelo de precificação ( pricing ) afeta o fluxo de caixa e a margem de contribuição do negócio. Evidence-Based Management (EBM): Adota as quatro Áreas-Chave de Valor ( Key Value Areas ) recomendadas pela Scrum.org: Current Value (CV): O valor que o produto gera hoje em receita, retenção e satisfação. Unrealized Value (UV): A oportunidade e a fatia de mercado ainda não capturadas. Time-to-Market (T2M): A velocidade do ciclo entre formular uma hipótese, colocá-la em produção e coletar dados reais de mercado. Ability to Innovate (A2I): A capacidade do time de inovar sem ser asfixiado por débito técnico ou processos burocráticos. Cost of Delay & Matriz de ROI: Toma decisões de priorização pautadas pelo Custo do Atraso ( Cost of Delay ), garantindo que a capacidade produtiva seja alocada onde o retorno ajustado pelo risco financeiro for maior. O Apoio da IA no Nível Marrom (Dashboards Preditivos e Analytics): O Faixa Marrom opera com modelos de IA preditiva que simulam o impacto de variações de preço, projetam o P&L em tempo real e detectam anomalias nas métricas de EBM antes que elas contaminem o balanço do trimestre. 3. Faixa Preta: A Visão do Empreendedor, Três Horizontes e a Cabeça de Ponte Na Faixa Preta, o Product Owner atinge o patamar executivo descrito por Ralph Jocham e Don McGreal: o PO como um verdadeiro empreendedor e tomador de riscos corporativo. Ele equilibra a sustentação do negócio presente com a conquista de novos mercados. Gestão de Portfólio em Três Horizontes: H1 (Core): Proteção, rentabilização e eficiência da vaca leiteira atual. H2 (Escalar): Aceleração de linhas de produtos adjacentes rumo ao crescimento em escala. H3 (Futuro): Apostas disruptivas e exploração de novas fronteiras de negócio. Crossing the Chasm e a Estratégia de Cabeça de Ponte ( Beachhead Market ): Para cruzar o temido abismo entre os entusiastas ( Early Adopters ) e a maioria pragmática ( Early Majority ), o Faixa Preta recusa a armadilha de tentar vender tudo para todo mundo. items.title: Wenn ich einen neuen Scrum-Leitfaden schreiben wollte
items.summary: Image Scrum Guide 2020 ist die neueste Version, fast sechs Jahre alt. In den letzten 6 Jahren hat sich der Markt enorm verändert, insbesondere mit dem Aufstieg der KI. Da in den letzten sechs Jahren weltweit Millionen von Menschen Scrum verwendet haben, bin ich mir sicher, dass es eine Menge Feedback gibt, das in Scrum integriert werden muss. Daher bin ich fest davon überzeugt, dass es an der Zeit ist, eine neue Version des Scrum Guide zu schreiben. Hier sind meine wichtigsten Änderungsvorschläge, wenn ich den Scrum Guide 2027 schreiben würde: #1 – Klarheit über Verantwortlichkeit, Verantwortung und Rolle Im Scrum Guide 2020 finden wir diesen Satz: „Scrum definiert drei spezifische Verantwortlichkeiten innerhalb des Scrum-Teams: die Entwickler, den Product Owner und den Scrum Master.“ Dieser Satz vermittelt jedoch fälschlicherweise die Vorstellung, dass es sich um drei Rollen im Scrum-Team handelt, während Verantwortlichkeiten und Rollen zwei verschiedene Dinge sind. Hier ist mein Vorschlag für die Änderung: Stellen Sie sich vor, Sie betreiben ein Restaurant und möchten Kunden mit Ihrer leckeren Pizza bedienen. Ihr Restaurant als Ganzes ist dafür verantwortlich, den Kunden heiße, gesunde und köstliche Pizza zu servieren. Um Ihre Kunden zu bedienen, müssen Sie Pizza kochen. Es gibt mehrere Aktivitäten oder Arbeiten, die Sie erledigen müssen, um das endgültige Gericht zu erhalten, wie z. B. Teigzubereitung, Soßenzubereitung, Zutaten wie Paprika, Pilze, Salami usw. hacken, Käse und andere Zutaten auf den Teig geben, den Teig in den Ofen geben, … Ich glaube, das ist eine Liste von Verantwortlichkeiten. Nun benötigen Sie einige Rollen, um diese Aktivitäten zu übernehmen und auszuführen. Es kann nur eine Rolle sein, die alle oben genannten Aktivitäten ausführt, oder es können mehrere Rollen sein, wie zum Beispiel: Teigbereiter, Saucenbereiter, Pizzabäcker und Ofenbereiter. Es hängt von der Größe und dem Umfang der Bestellungen Ihres Restaurants ab, oder besser gesagt von Ihrem Kontext. Lassen Sie mich es nun dem Scrum-Kontext zuordnen. Verantwortlichkeit: Das Scrum-Team als Ganzes ist dafür verantwortlich, ein Qualitätsprodukt zu entwickeln und bereitzustellen, um zufriedene Stakeholder und Kunden zu gewinnen. Verantwortlichkeiten: Ich glaube, dass es vier Hauptkategorien von Verantwortlichkeiten gibt, darunter: Product Ownership: Die Aufgabe, die sicherstellt, dass das Team an der richtigen Sache arbeitet, um den Wert des Produkts zu maximieren. Entwicklung und Lieferung: Der Job, der das verwendbare Produkt erstellt und liefert. Scrum-Etablierung: Die Aufgabe, die die wahre Scrum-Arbeitsweise etabliert und die Effektivität des Scrum-Teams im Laufe der Zeit verbessert. KI-Orchestrierung: Der Job, der KI in die Scrum-Arbeitsweise des Teams integriert. Rollen: Auf dem Markt gibt es viele Namen und Ausdrücke, die für Personen verwendet werden, die die genannten Aktivitäten ausführen, wie zum Beispiel: Für Product Ownership: Product Owner, Produktmanager, Projektmanager, … Für Entwicklung und Bereitstellung: Entwickler, Back-End-Entwickler, Front-End-Entwickler, UI/UX-Designer, Tester, Qualitätssicherung, … Für Scrum Establishment: Scrum Master, Agile Coach, Scrum Coach, Delivery Manager, … Für AI Orchestration: Da KI neu ist, gibt es keinen spezifischen Namen dafür dieser Kategorie. Scrum sollte keine Rolle vorschreiben, da es stark kontextorientiert ist. Beispielsweise ist es möglich, dass in einem Scrum-Team eine Person sowohl die Verantwortung für die Scrum-Einrichtung als auch für die KI-Orchestrierung übernimmt. Dann können Sie es nennen, wie Sie wollen. Da das Scrum-Team ein sich selbst verwaltendes Team ist und für das Endergebnis verantwortlich ist, sollten sie ihre kollektive Intelligenz nutzen, Rollen (oder möglicherweise werden Rollen von der Organisation definiert) in ihrem Scrum-Team definieren und diesen Rollen Verantwortlichkeiten zuweisen. #2 – Daily Scrum-zu-Alignment-Ereignis Wenn das Daily Scrum an jedem Arbeitstag durchgeführt wird, besteht ein hohes Potenzial, dass es in eine Aufgabe umgewandelt wird, die ein Häkchen erhalten sollte. Ich glaube, es sollte immer dann passieren, wenn es nötig ist und wenn das erste Teammitglied die Hand hebt, die ausgerichtet werden muss. Deshalb habe ich das Wort „Täglich“ in „Ausrichtung“ geändert, damit es nicht als Ereignis wahrgenommen wird, das täglich stattfinden sollte. Darüber hinaus sollte es nicht nur für Entwickler obligatorisch sein. Es sollte für alle Teammitglieder verpflichtend sein. Wenn also ein Mitglied die Hand hebt, weil etwas Neues passiert ist, muss es etwas mit dem Team teilen, oder es ist ein Hindernis aufgetreten; Dann versammelt sich das gesamte Team am selben Ort und zur gleichen Zeit, um sich abzustimmen. Dieser Vorschlag entspringt meiner tiefen und langjährigen Erfahrung. #3 – Value Backlog und Definition of Value (DoV) Mit dem Aufkommen der KI ist die Entwicklung des Produkts nicht länger der Engpass. Stattdessen besteht das Hauptanliegen der Scrum-Teams darin, zu erkennen, was einen echten Mehrwert bietet. Daher ist ein neues Konzept der Definition of Value (DoV) erforderlich. Das Scrum-Team sollte ein kristallklares Bild davon haben, was Wert ist. Darüber hinaus füge ich dem Scrum-Framework ein neues Backlog hinzu, das Value Backlog heißt. Dabei handelt es sich um eine Liste von Product Backlog Items, die bereits freigegeben wurden und von den Kunden verwendet werden. Das heißt, wenn Kunden einen PBI nicht als echten Wert akzeptieren oder ihn nicht mehr verwenden, sollte dieser PBI aus dem Value Backlog entfernt werden. items.origTitle: If I Wanted To Write A New Scrum Guide
items.origSummary: Image Scrum Guide 2020 is the latest version, nearly six years old. Over the past 6 years, the market has changed enormously, especially with the rise of AI. With millions of people using Scrum worldwide over the past 6 years, I am sure there is a lot of feedback that needs to be incorporated into Scrum. So, I strongly believe it is time to write a new version of the Scrum Guide. Here are my main suggested changes if I were to write the Scrum Guide 2027: #1- Clarity on Accountability, Responsibility, and Role In the Scrum Guide 2020, we have this sentence: “Scrum defines three specific accountabilities within the Scrum Team: the Developers, the Product Owner, and the Scrum Master.” However, this sentence mistakenly conveys the idea that they are three roles in the Scrum Team, while accountabilities and roles are two different things. Here is my suggestion for the change: Imagine you run a restaurant and want to serve customers with your delicious pizza. Your restaurant as a whole is accountable for serving customers with hot, healthy, and delicious pizza. To serve your customers, you need to cook pizza. There are several activities or jobs you need to do to get the final dish, like dough preparation, sauce preparation, chopping ingredients like bell peppers, mushrooms, salami, etc., adding cheese and other ingredients on top of the dough, putting the dough into the oven, … I believe these are a list of responsibilities. Now, you need some roles to take over and do these activities. It can be just one role that does all the above activities, or it can be several roles like: Dough Maker, Sauce Maker, Pizza Maker, and Oven Tender. It depends on the size and volume of the orders of your restaurant, or better to say your context. Now, let me map it to the Scrum context. Accountability: The Scrum Team as a whole is accountable for developing and delivering a quality product to build satisfied stakeholders and customers. Responsibilities: I believe there are four main categories of responsibilities, including: Product Ownership : The job that makes sure that the team is working on the right thing to maximize the value of the product. Development & Delivery : The job that builds and delivers the usable product. Scrum Establishment : The job that establishes the true Scrum way of working and improves the Scrum Team’s effectiveness over time. AI Orchestration : The job that incorporates AI into the Scrum way of working of the team. Roles: In the market, there are a lot of names and phrases that are used for people who do the mentioned activities, such as: For Product Ownership : Product Owner, Product Manager, Project Manager, … For Development & Delivery: Developer, Back-end Developer, Front-end Developer, UI/UX Designer, Tester, Quality Assurance, … For Scrum Establishment : Scrum Master, Agile Coach, Scrum Coach, Delivery Manager, … For AI Orchestration : as AI is new, there is no specific name for this category. Scrum should not prescribe any role, as it is heavily context-oriented. As an example, it is possible that in a Scrum Team, one person takes over both the Scrum Establishment and AI Orchestration responsibilities. Then you can call it whatever you want. As the Scrum Team is a self-managing team and accountable for the final result, they should leverage their collective intelligence, define roles (or maybe roles are defined by the organization) in their Scrum Team and assign responsibilities to those roles. #2- Daily Scrum to Alignment Event When the Daily Scrum is run on every working day, it has a high potential to be converted into a task that should get a checkmark. I believe it should happen whenever it is needed and when the first team member raises their hand that needs alignment. So, I changed the word Daily to Alignment to not perceived as an event that should happen on a daily basis. In addition, it shouldn’t be mandatory for just Developers. It should be mandatory for all team members. So, when a member raises their hand because something new happened, they need to share something with the team, or an impediment occurred; then the whole team gathers in the same place and time to get aligned. This suggestion comes from my deep and long experience. #3- Value Backlog & Definition of Value (DoV) With the advent of AI, building the product is no longer the bottleneck. Instead, Scrum Teams' main concern is to recognize what to build that delivers real value. So, a new concept of Definition of Value (DoV) is needed. Scrum Team should have a crystal-clear picture of what value is. In addition, I add a new backlog to the Scrum framework that is called Value Backlog. It is a list of Product Backlog Items that have already been released and are being used by the customers. items.title: Your AI agents can deliver; Scrum is what governs them
items.summary: Scrum governs three things: who decides what gets built, what counts as finished, and how the rules change when they stop working. For eighteen months, I have been Product Owner of a Scrum Team of eight AI agents, the Relentless Raptors . At our current token budget, the team completes roughly 10 times as many Product Backlog items in a one-week Sprint as a human team would (Hodgson & West, 2026a). Capacity stopped being the constraint long ago, and governance is now the only thing keeping the output pointed at the Product Goal. Agents have no informal channels Human teams compensate for weak governance through everyday interaction: an overheard conversation, a colleague reviewing a draft, the social pressure that holds a norm in place without anyone writing it down. Agents have none of those channels. Each session opens a fresh context window with no memory of the last one and no standing among peers, and an agent holds no tacit knowledge to fall back on (Nonaka & Takeuchi, 1995). Weak governance in an agent team therefore produces no visible argument. It produces silent failure, where every output passes its acceptance criteria while the work as a whole drifts away from the goal it was meant to serve (Hodgson & West, 2026a). Research on multi-agent systems locates the problem in the same place. Across 7 multi-agent frameworks, 41.8% of observed failures originated in specification and system design (Cemri et al., 2025). The authors traced these failures largely to design choices, including how agent roles and workflows were set up and how tasks were specified. Improving role specifications alone raised one framework's task success rate by 9.4% on the same model (Cemri et al., 2025). The failures lay in the system's design, which is where Scrum does its work. Human teams are not exempt from any of this. Informal channels let a human team run on an unclear Sprint Goal or a Definition of Done nobody reads; agents remove that cover, and whatever Scrum is doing for a team becomes plain to see. The Scrum Guide needs no additions to govern the Raptors. What changes is the form: every commitment and every norm has to exist as a document an agent reads before it acts. The Product Owner sets direction Direction starts with the team canvas. Scrum's three commitments, the Product Goal, the Sprint Goal and the Definition of Done (Schwaber & Sutherland, 2020), appear on the canvas as an order of obligation: the Product Goal is fixed, the Sprint Goal that serves it is fixed, the Definition of Done is immutable, and only the method of doing a task is flexible (Hodgson, 2026). The order exists because an agent's default is to finish a task by any available means, including breaking its own rules. For agents, the canvas is the complete statement of norms, since no other source of norms exists. It also records each agent's domain, the limits of its authority and its escalation path (Hodgson & West, 2026b). Ordering the Product Backlog is the first decision I keep. A team producing at 10 times human pace turns a stale Product Backlog into a large volume of finished work nobody needs, so I reorder it as soon as new evidence arrives rather than waiting for the next Sprint. The Sprint Review tests that ordering. The Scrum Guide says the Scrum Team presents the Sprint results to key stakeholders and decides with them what to do next (Schwaber & Sutherland, 2020). For the Raptors, readers' response to the published work, drawn from site, LinkedIn and email engagement data, sits alongside the Increment, and the question is whether the Sprint Goal advanced the Product Goal and whether the team is still solving the right problem. Agents do not tire, so the strain on sustainable pace runs the other way: production outruns the Product Owner's capacity to make sense of it and steer. The Review is the pause protecting that capacity (Hodgson & West, 2026d), and it ends with a reordered Product Backlog. Release is the second decision I keep. It sits at the irreversibility boundary, the point at which the consequences of a wrong decision can no longer be corrected in the product's next iteration (Hodgson, 2026). Every Raptors item stops one step short of publication. Below the boundary, agents work under bounded authority; above it, I review the evidence and decide what to release. One file decides what is finished The Scrum Guide makes the Definition of Done the commitment for the Increment, and an item failing it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review (Schwaber & Sutherland, 2020). For the Raptors, the Definition of Done is one versioned file with criteria across eleven domains, and it is the only completion authority. The team learned the value of a single file by running two. For four months in 2026, two copies of the Definition of Done evolved in parallel until both carried the number v1.3, and agents worked to whichever copy they had read last. Any second copy is now treated as a defect, and every Product Backlog…

items.title: Fourteen Ways to Stop Lying to Yourself: the Wizard's Rules in One place
items.summary: Fourteen Wizard’s Rules ago, this series made a claim: most agile failures aren’t failures of process, they’re failures of honesty. An organization rarely breaks because it skipped a ceremony. It breaks because it avoided a reality, protected a story, or kept doing something nobody could justify, and dressed all of it in the language of transformation. Fourteen Rules later, the claim has had its say. And the strange thing, looking back across all of them, is how little of it was ever really about agile. Goodkind wrote these for wizards and wars. They turned out to describe steering committees and standups with uncomfortable precision, because they were never about magic. They were about the one discipline underneath all professional work: refusing to lie to yourself. That’s what the fourteen Rules are, in the end. One Rule in fourteen costumes. Stop lying to yourself. The three arcs Read in order, the Rules move through three stages, and the movement is the argument. The first five are about how you get fooled. The comfortable lie you want to believe, the harm that grows out of good intentions, the passion that drowns the evidence, the missing forgiveness that drives the truth underground, and the deeds that quietly reveal what an organization actually values, whatever its poster says. The next five are about the discipline that pulls you back out. Letting reason rule instead of ritual, facing forward instead of relitigating old defeats, earning an outcome instead of wishing for it, refusing the contradictions you’ve been calling balance, and acting on the truth you’ve already seen instead of stepping politely around it. The last four are the harder edges, the ones most agile writing avoids. Holding your strength without letting it curdle into contempt. Knowing that silencing a truth never touches the truth. Setting a boundary against the people who actually want the work to fail. And choosing how you act inside a system you can’t fully change, because that choice is the one thing it can never make for you. The eight fundamentals underneath Every one of the fourteen lands in the same place: the fundamentals underneath, and usually more than one of them. There are eight in all, the behaviors a professional organization runs on, and no framework can install them for you. Reality Transparency, seeing the true state of the work. Honest Inspection, confronting it against what you promised. Decisive Adaptation, changing course on the evidence. Trust and Candor, making it safe to say the hard true thing. Outcome Ownership, owning the result and not just the tickets. Decision Mandate, pairing the authority to decide with responsibility for the outcome. Skill Completeness, having what it takes to do the work without rescue. Commitment to Quality, building it in rather than trading it away under pressure. The Rules are fourteen alarms, each going off when one or more of those fundamentals start to fail. Which is why the most useful way to read what follows isn’t as a list of ideas. It’s as a diagnostic. Run your own organization past it, slowly, and notice which alarms are already ringing. And read it as a leader, because leadership holds the biggest levers here. Several of the eight, the authority a team holds, what the budget rewards, whether the truth is safe to send upward, what’s allowed to end, are mostly set above the team, by the people who sponsor and fund the work. But this isn’t only a leadership job. A team can act on every one of these within the mandate it already has, and anyone on it can lead from where they stand. The structure is leadership’s to move; the choosing starts anywhere. So read the list that follows as a checklist for whoever is holding it. The fourteen, in one place Each one below gives the lie it catches, the exact Wizard’s Rule it reads from, the name this series gave the failure, the fundamentals underneath, and the one question that exposes it. The title is only one way into the rule; the rule itself is the broader thing. Read for the questions, though. They’re the part you can use tomorrow. 1. You believe the transformation worked because you want it to. The Rule: “People will believe a lie because they want it to be true, or because they’re afraid it might be true.” Hope and fear, not evidence, drive the green dashboard. The belief with a budget . Fundamentals: Reality Transparency, Honest Inspection. Ask: what would have to be true for us to admit this isn’t working, and have we actually checked? 2. Your best-intentioned help built a dependent team. The Rule: “The greatest harm can result from the best intentions.” Rescue, not support, strips a team of its ownership. Kind dependence . Fundamentals: Outcome Ownership, Decision Mandate, Skill Completeness. Ask: if we disappeared tomorrow, would this team be more capable, or just stuck? 3. Your most passionate decisions are your worst ones. The Rule: “Passion rules reason, for better or for worse.” Conviction quietly switches off…

items.title: Studie: Leben auf Saturnmond denkbar
items.summary: Trotz eisiger Kälte und kaum Sauerstoff ist der Saturnmond Enceladus laut einer neuen Studie lebensfreundlicher als bisher angenommen. In seinem verborgenen Ozean könnten Mikroorganismen überleben.

items.title: Diese Diät kann die Alterung des Gehirns um 2,5 Jahre verlangsamen
items.summary: Menschen, die die MIND-Diät genauer befolgten, zeigten im Laufe der Zeit eine langsamere Schrumpfung des Gehirns und einen geringeren Verlust der grauen Substanz, wobei die stärksten Unterschiede einer etwa 2,5 Jahre verzögerten Gehirnalterung entsprachen. Beeren und Geflügel wurden mit gesünderen Gehirnveränderungen in Verbindung gebracht, während Süßigkeiten und frittiertes Fastfood mit einem größeren Gewebeverlust in Verbindung gebracht wurden.
items.origTitle: This diet may slow brain aging by 2.5 years
items.origSummary: People who followed the MIND diet more closely showed slower brain shrinkage and less grey matter loss over time, with the strongest differences equivalent to about 2.5 years of delayed brain aging. Berries and poultry were linked with healthier brain changes, while sweets and fried fast foods were associated with greater tissue loss.

items.title: Schon Urzellen konnten herumkriechen
items.summary: Bereits vor rund zwei Milliarden Jahren sind die Vorläufer aller Tiere, Pflanzen und Pilze offenbar herumgekrochen: In zwanzig Minuten können Asgard-Archaeen genannte Urzellen auf diese Weise 0,06 Millimeter zurücklegen, fand ein Forschungsteam der Universität Wien nun heraus.

items.title: Vorschulkinder schaffen 18.000 Schritte
items.summary: Kleine Kinder sind deutlich bewegungsaktiver, als viele Erwachsene vermuten: Circa 18.000 Schritte am Tag sind im Alter von drei bis vier Jahren typisch. Das ergab eine internationale Studie mit mehr als 3.500 Kindern in 44 Ländern.

items.title: Könnte der Verzicht auf hochverarbeitete Lebensmittel Ihre geistige Gesundheit verbessern?
items.summary: Menschen mit Depressionen, die stark auf hochverarbeitete Lebensmittel verzichteten, erlebten in einer kleinen vorläufigen Studie bemerkenswerte Verbesserungen ihrer Symptome. Forscher vermuten, dass eine gesündere Ernährung dem Gehirn zugute kommen kann, indem sie unter anderem Darmschäden und chronische Entzündungen reduziert.
items.origTitle: Could quitting ultra-processed food boost your mental health?
items.origSummary: People with depression who dramatically cut ultra-processed foods experienced notable improvements in their symptoms in a small preliminary study. Researchers suspect healthier eating may benefit the brain partly by reducing gut damage and chronic inflammation.

items.title: Armut nahm EU-weit ab
items.summary: In der EU ist die Armut zwischen 2015 und 2023 zurückgegangen. Das ergibt eine aktuelle Studie der Wirtschaftsuniversität Bratislava auf Basis verfügbarer Daten. Allerdings gibt es regionale Unterschiede. Österreich liegt bei der Armutsbekämpfung im EU-Vergleich im oberen Mittelfeld.

items.title: Muster auf Flügeln verwirren Angreifer
items.summary: Schmetterlinge fliegen vergleichsweise langsam und wären eigentlich eine leichte Beute. Trotzdem haben Vögel Probleme damit, sie im Flug zu fangen. Laut einer aktuellen Studie liegt das an den Mustern auf den Flügeln der Insekten. Im Flug erzeugen sie eine optische Täuschung, die Angreifer in die Irre führt.

items.title: Ein rekordverdächtiger Röntgenblitz könnte die Geburt eines Magnetars offenbaren
items.summary: Astronomen haben starke Beweise dafür gefunden, dass einige mysteriöse, minutenlange Röntgenblitze entstehen, wenn zwei Neutronensterne kollidieren und einen Magnetar erzeugen. Ein rekordverdächtiges Ereignis leuchtete fast zehn Minuten lang im Röntgenlicht und eröffnete möglicherweise einen neuen Weg, diese extremen kosmischen Verschmelzungen zu finden.
items.origTitle: A record-breaking X-ray flash may reveal the birth of a magnetar
items.origSummary: Astronomers have found strong evidence that some mysterious, minutes-long X-ray flashes are produced when two neutron stars collide and create a magnetar. One record-setting event glowed in X-rays for nearly 10 minutes, potentially opening a new way to find these extreme cosmic mergers.

items.title: Kettenverträge: Doktorat als neue Schwelle
items.summary: Entgegen dem allgemeinen Arbeitsrecht sind an Universitäten mehrmalige Aneinanderreihungen von befristeten Verträgen erlaubt. Dieser „Kettenvertrags-Paragraf“ im Universitätsgesetz soll nun geändert werden. Ab dem Doktorat sollen keine Befristungen mehr erlaubt sein.

items.title: Maulbeere kann Darmbakterien umgestalten und den Stoffwechsel beeinflussen
items.summary: Maulbeerverbindungen können das Darmmikrobiom auf eine Weise umgestalten, die die Darmgesundheit und den Stoffwechsel unterstützt, wobei einige Kombinationen in Tierversuchen besonders starke Wirkungen zeigten. Allerdings variieren die Ergebnisse je nach Pflanzenteil und Verarbeitungsmethode, und die Vorteile beim Menschen müssen noch bestätigt werden.
items.origTitle: Mulberry may reshape gut bacteria and influence metabolism
items.origSummary: Mulberry compounds may reshape the gut microbiome in ways that support intestinal health and metabolism, with some combinations showing especially strong effects in animal studies. However, the results vary depending on the plant part and processing method, and the benefits have yet to be confirmed in humans.

items.title: Der Marsrover Perseverance der NASA findet Grundwasser, Seen und heiße Flüssigkeiten an einem Ort
items.summary: Der Perseverance-Rover der NASA hat eine überraschend komplizierte Geschichte des Wassers im Jezero-Krater aufgedeckt. Wissenschaftler gingen davon aus, dass die Randeinheit des Kraters Seesedimente enthalten würde, fanden jedoch stattdessen uraltes magmatisches Gestein, das bei mindestens drei verschiedenen Gelegenheiten durch Wasser verändert wurde.
items.origTitle: NASA's Perseverance Mars rover finds groundwater, lakes, and hot fluids in one place
items.origSummary: NASA’s Perseverance rover has uncovered a surprisingly complicated history of water in Jezero Crater. Scientists expected the crater’s Margin Unit to contain lake sediments, but instead found ancient igneous rocks that were altered by water on at least three separate occasions.

items.title: Jets von Schwarzen Löchern könnten über das Schicksal ganzer Galaxien entscheiden
items.summary: Mächtige Jets von supermassiven Schwarzen Löchern können sternbildendes Gas weit über den sichtbaren Rand einer Galaxie hinaus stören und eine leuchtende Spur hinterlassen, die Hunderttausende Lichtjahre lang ist. Indem sie dieses Gas heiß halten und verhindern, dass es nach innen fällt, können die Jets dabei helfen, festzustellen, ob in einer Galaxie weiterhin Sterne entstehen oder ob sie still wird.
items.origTitle: Black hole jets may decide the fate of entire galaxies
items.origSummary: Powerful jets from supermassive black holes can disturb star-forming gas far beyond a galaxy’s visible edge, leaving a glowing trail hundreds of thousands of light-years long. By keeping this gas hot and preventing it from falling inward, the jets may help determine whether a galaxy keeps forming stars or becomes quiet.

items.title: Live ansehen: Die Crew-13 der NASA könnte die schnellste US-Reise zur ISS aller Zeiten unternehmen
items.summary: Die SpaceX-Crew-13-Mission der NASA soll am 1. Oktober vier Astronauten zur Internationalen Raumstation befördern. Der Dragon könnte das umlaufende Labor in nur 7 Stunden und 50 Minuten erreichen und wäre damit die schnellste Reise eines US-Raumschiffs zur ISS in der Geschichte.
items.origTitle: Watch Live: NASA’s Crew-13 could make the fastest U.S. trip to the ISS ever
items.origSummary: NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission is scheduled to launch four astronauts to the International Space Station on October 1. The Dragon could reach the orbiting laboratory in just 7 hours and 50 minutes, making it the fastest U.S. spacecraft journey to the ISS in history.

items.title: Der NASA-Rover Curiosity hat gerade 5.000 Tage auf dem Mars verbracht und dieses atemberaubende Bild zurückgesendet
items.summary: Der NASA-Rover Curiosity markierte 5.000 Marstage, indem er Morgen- und Nachmittagsansichten einfing, die zu einer eindrucksvollen Mars-„Postkarte“ zusammengefügt wurden. Das Panorama zeigt Curiosity, seine Spuren und die riesige Landschaft rund um Mount Sharp und Gale Crater.
items.origTitle: NASA’s Curiosity rover just hit 5,000 days on Mars and sent back this stunning view
items.origSummary: NASA’s Curiosity rover marked 5,000 Martian days by capturing morning and afternoon views that were blended into a striking Mars “postcard.” The panorama shows Curiosity, its tracks, and the enormous landscape surrounding Mount Sharp and Gale Crater.

items.title: Forscher finden heraus, dass Kreatin auch ohne körperliche Betätigung beim Muskelaufbau helfen kann
items.summary: In einer neuen 12-wöchigen Studie half Kreatin Erwachsenen mittleren Alters, auch ohne strukturiertes Trainingsprogramm Muskeln und Kraft aufzubauen. In Kombination mit Bewegung und einer kalorienreduzierten Ernährung führte es zu noch größeren Kraftzuwächsen und half den Teilnehmern gleichzeitig dabei, mageres Gewebe aufzubauen und Fett zu verlieren. Forscher sagen, dass die Ergebnisse die Argumente dafür untermauern, dass Kreatin ein potenziell nützliches Hilfsmittel für den Muskelerhalt mit zunehmendem Alter ist.
items.origTitle: Creatine may help build muscle even without exercise, researchers find
items.origSummary: Creatine helped middle-aged adults gain muscle and strength even without a structured workout program in a new 12-week study. When combined with exercise and a calorie-reduced diet, it produced even greater strength gains while helping participants add lean tissue and lose fat. Researchers say the results strengthen the case for creatine as a potentially useful tool for maintaining muscle with age.
